title: Keep-Right-Except-to-Pass Rule Evaluation and Traffic-Rule Design

limitations: All 30 PDF pages are text-extracted, rendered, and visually reviewed.
PDF p1 is Summary and p2 is Contents; Contents is not author-language evidence.
PDF p30 contains a Conclusion continuation above the References heading, so only the References portion is excluded.
PDF p14-p16 are dominated by diagrams; their flowchart nodes are visual/algorithm evidence, not natural-language units.
Extraction has mojibake in some quote marks and symbols, so central formulas were compared with rendered pages.

deliverables: Evaluate keep-right-except-to-pass in light and heavy traffic using five criteria.
Construct and compare better traffic rules.
Test whether the selected rule transfers to left-hand traffic.
Assess how intelligent driving control changes the conclusions.
task_reconstruction.reconstruction_limit: No official problem statement was located in the source directory, so task wording is reconstructed only from the paper.

section_map.summary: Four-paragraph route from baseline rule to evaluation, CA, AHP selection, extensions, and recommendation.
Navigation only; excluded from positive language evidence.
Context, four deliverables, and dependency roadmap.
Traffic, road, vehicle, speed, and arrival-process scope.
Five metrics, units, and preferred directions.
CA assumptions, representation, algorithm, outputs, validation, and sensitivity.
Candidate rules, common simulation, normalization, AHP, and Rule 2 selection.
LHT orientation transfer and IDS extension.

Synthesis and conditional result recap; continues on PDF p30.

contributions.summary: Defines five criterion directions before judging a traffic rule.
Uses a state transition argument to identify a lowest-speed absorbing outcome.
Explains why return-space loss breaks the light model and the rule itself.
Builds a two-lane discrete simulator with rule-specific Go and Return behavior.
Creates three explicit alternatives from baseline failure mechanisms.
Uses direction-aware normalization and a consistent AHP matrix to select Rule 2.
Separates orientation mirroring from intelligent-control assumptions.

edges: light and heavy theories -> CA validation targets
raw alternative outputs -> normalization and AHP
feedbacks: Sensitivity tables are intended to bound CA confidence.
Extension tests are intended to limit rather than universally generalize Rule 2.
dependency_graph.closure_status: The positive route from task to decision is explicit. Exact CA reproduction is limited by missing seeds, observation details, and contradictory horizon/lambda statements.

assumptions.summary: Drivers are rational; road conditions are normal.
Right-side traffic, two forward lanes, four-lane freeway, and separated opposing directions.
No lights, intersections, exits, or sharp turns.
Free speed is constant until instantaneous reaction to a car ahead.
Entry intervals are exponential and arrivals Poisson.
One-second time step, discrete uniform speeds, and a two-second safe-distance coefficient.
IDS observes all vehicles and makes overtaking absolutely safe under its stated conditions.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Traffic outputs are defined rather than drawn from an external data set.
CA generates Poisson arrivals at the right-lane entrance.
Cells store zero for empty space and positive integer vehicle speed.
Counts and speeds are accumulated from first arrival at an observation point.
Plots vary lambda and Table 1 reports lambda 0.25 and 0.4.
Table 5 uses lambda 0.25, while p25 later claims 0.3.
Criteria are normalized by direction before AHP aggregation.

models.summary: MU-A-2014-29282-001: Define comparable traffic performance before judging rules.
MU-A-2014-29282-002: Derive the long-run light-traffic state under keep-right-except-to-pass.
MU-A-2014-29282-003: Explain why the light-state transition model ceases to apply in congested traffic.
MU-A-2014-29282-004: Encode the freeway, arrivals, and vehicles as a finite discrete state space.
MU-A-2014-29282-005: Operationalize keep-right-except-to-pass through Go and Return stages.
MU-A-2014-29282-006: Convert CA trajectories into comparable traffic metrics and response curves.
MU-A-2014-29282-007: Create and compare three lane-allocation and overtaking alternatives under the CA.
MU-A-2014-29282-008: Convert unlike and oppositely directed criteria into a weighted comprehensive index.
MU-A-2014-29282-009: Test whether Rule 2 and the baseline rule retain their behavior under left-hand orientation and an intelligent driving system.

verification.summary: One numerical iteration uses p1=.35, p2=.45, p3=.29, and initial proportions .2/.5/.3 to reach the stated absorbing vector.
Light and heavy screenshots are used as qualitative mirrors of the two theory outcomes.
One-at-a-time p1, p2, and d perturbations show the stated local sensitivity.
Independent recomputation of displayed reciprocal matrix agrees with CI=.0223, CR=.0199, and Table 8 weights to rounding.
Source claims Rule 2 remains best at lambda .2 and .4 without showing the data.
Figures 19-22 compare four outputs under IDS and no IDS, but no numerical data or repetition evidence is supplied.

results_trace.summary: State model and Figure 3 yield the claimed long-run (0,0,1) proportion vector.
Return-space loss produces lane-specific v3/v4 behavior and rule violation.
Table 1 and Figures 10-14 relate five criteria to lambda.
Figures 15-16 connect simulation configurations to light/heavy analytical claims.
Table 5 supplies raw values for old rule and Rules 1-3.
Table 6 and Figure 17 make Rule 2 a provisional visual leader.
Table 9 assigns Rule 2 the highest EIC=.9219.
LHT is mirrored; IDS output comparisons are conditional on traffic regime.

writing_logic.summary: baseline gap -> five criteria -> two-regime theory -> CA cross-check -> alternative design/AHP -> extension -> recommendation
capacity and safety context -> operating rule -> four deliverables -> dependency roadmap -> Figure 1
real traffic complexity -> explicit exclusions -> controlled road/vehicle/arrival world
informal light/heavy labels -> operational condition -> five metric definitions and directions
states and probabilities -> transition matrix -> bound/limit -> numerical check -> low-speed implication
light-model premise fails -> safe-distance mechanism -> different steady state -> CA handoff
assumptions and state space -> Go/Return algorithm -> measurement protocol -> results
theory claim -> matched lambda scenario -> screenshot correspondence -> local support
baseline failures -> three candidate mechanisms -> shared CA output -> anomaly explanation
unit/polarity mismatch -> normalized indices -> radar precheck -> AHP consistency -> EIC choice
right-side and human-judgment assumptions -> LHT mirror / IDS revision -> regime-qualified outputs
cross-check strength -> concrete scope limits -> ordered recap and conditional advice

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: A four-paragraph summary that pairs methods, results, extensions, and limits may improve traceability, but award status is not causal judge evidence.
A visible logic framework may help a reviewer inspect task-to-decision handoffs, but no judge commentary establishes preference.
Showing the reciprocal matrix and CR makes a subjective weighting choice auditable, but the paper does not show why that mattered to judges.

weaknesses.summary: Text says T=1000 seconds while Figure 8 initializes T=2000.
Table 5 uses lambda=.25; p25 says this section arbitrarily set lambda=.3.
Starting observation at first arrival makes TF exceed lambda under a shortened denominator.
km/h definitions, m/s examples, cell units, and ATS table values are not reconciled.
Text compares speed difference with L m/s while Figure 9 uses a +1 cell comparison.
Rule 2 automatically receives SI=1 because DI is defined only as lane-change count.
Text predicts a heavy-traffic reversal while Figure 20 shows IDS ATS above non-IDS throughout its displayed range.
IDS heavy-state text cites subsection 3.1 instead of 3.3.
Orientation mirroring has no independent CA/AHP rerun or quantitative target evidence.
One-at-a-time perturbations do not establish coupled uncertainty or recommendation stability.

independent_extensions.summary: Replace lane-change count with a calibrated conflict-risk model including relative speed, headway, merge conflict, and severity.
Estimate a density/return-opportunity threshold from simulation or empirical data rather than defining light/heavy only descriptively.
Specify synchronous update order, collision resolution, speed support, observation point, seed, and replications.
Use global coupled sampling, repeated simulations, confidence intervals, and probability of winner reversal.
Elicit stakeholders, publish the matrix, run weight sensitivity, and compare AHP to data-derived/robust alternatives.
Re-estimate model inputs and test mirror symmetry empirically before applying the LHT recommendation.
Specify controller objective, return deadline, safety model, and handoff interface before simulating automation.
